GasGas’s stock targets for your 2023 MC 250F are:
- **Static sag: 35 mm (1.38 in)** — bike upright on its wheels, no rider.
- **Rider sag: 105 mm (4.13 in)** — you seated in your normal position, wearing full riding gear, feet on the pegs.

Both are measured as the drop from fully extended suspension, using the rear axle and the same rear-fender reference point. Have a helper hold and measure the bike, and settle the suspension before each reading.

Set rider sag first, then check static sag. General tuning rule: too little static sag with correct rider sag points to a shock spring that’s too soft; too much points to one that’s too stiff.
Target 35 mm static sag and 105 mm rider sag on your 2023 GasGas MC 250F.

That combination often means the fork is **too soft and riding deep**, where it feels harsh but still lacks landing support. Backing compression out further can make both problems worse.

1. **Fork air:** check it cold with the front wheel off the ground. GASGAS’s stock reference is **10.4 bar (151 psi)**; record your pressure before changing anything. Bleed the separate outer-chamber bleeders, not the spring-air valve, and check for sticky movement or leaks.
2. **Fork compression:** if it dives and rides deep, turn it **2 clicks in from your current position** for more hold-up. If currently at the stock **12 clicks out**, test **10 out**. Leave rebound unchanged for this test.

Ride the same chop and a familiar landing for a few laps. Keep the change if it rides higher, feels calmer and bottoms less; return to baseline if it deflects more without improving support. If it barely moves on chop yet bottoms only on big hits, don’t keep adding compression—that points toward separate small-bump and end-stroke tuning.

Rear balance matters too: stock targets are **105 mm rider sag / 35 mm static sag**. What do you weigh in riding gear?

**Changes to try, one at a time:**
- **Fork compression:** If the fork dives and rides deep, turn 2 clicks in from the current position; from 12 to 10 clicks out only if currently at the stock reference.
Harsh chop plus bottoming often means the fork is riding too deep—not simply too stiff. Verify cold air pressure before softening the compression.

Hard braking dive usually means the fork needs more spring or compression support—not softer damping.

1. **Check fork air first:** GasGas’s stock reference is **10.4 bar (151 psi)**. Check cold with the front wheel off the ground; release trapped air through the separate outer-chamber bleeders, not the main air valve. This is the stock reference, not a weight-specific recommendation.
2. Check rear balance: **105 mm rider sag and 35 mm static sag** are the stock targets. A rear sitting too high loads the fork more.
3. **Fork compression: turn in two clicks from your current position**. If it’s at the stock 12 clicks out, go from **12 to 10 out**. Leave rebound alone; its stock reference is 12 out.

Retest the same braking zone for a few laps. You want less dive without sharp hits through the bars; return two clicks if it becomes harsh or pushes wide without improving support.

For technique, brace with your legs and move your hips back over the pegs before progressively squeezing the brake. Practise five controlled straight-line stops at an easy pace.

**Changes to try, one at a time:**
- **Fork compression:** Turn in two clicks from the current position; if currently at stock, from 12 to 10 clicks out.
Check the fork’s cold air pressure first, then try fork compression two clicks firmer for more braking support.

**One click at a time** is the best testing step on your 2022 CRF250R—testers consistently find this suspension sensitive to small changes. Two clicks can make the difference clearer, but use one when fine-tuning.

- **Clockwise/in:** more damping—firmer compression or slower rebound.
- **Counterclockwise/out:** less damping—softer compression or faster rebound.
- **Shock high-speed compression:** Honda specifies **1/12 turn at a time**, not clicks.

Write down your starting position, change only one adjuster, then ride the same section for a few laps at a consistent pace. Keep both fork legs matched. If it gets worse, return to your starting setting before testing anything else; count positions from lightly seated, never forced.

**That points to shock fade—not simply settings that are too soft.** As the shock heats up, weak compression damping lets it sink and weak rebound damping lets it bounce. Some temperature change is normal; a pronounced loss of control isn’t.

Most likely, in order:
1. **Degraded or aerated shock oil**, losing damping as it gets hot.
2. **Low nitrogen charge or a separator sealing problem**, allowing the oil to foam.
3. **Worn internal seals**, letting more oil bypass the damping circuits when hot.

With the bike cold and engine off, inspect the shock shaft and body for oil leakage. Then arrange a shock service: oil condition, nitrogen retention, separator and piston seals need checking—not just a recharge. If the rear also sits lower after riding, Honda specifically calls for checking nitrogen loss.

Don’t tighten the clickers to hide it or ride another moto once it becomes uncontrolled.

**How many riding hours since the shock was last serviced?** The hot-only change makes service the priority either way.
A shock that becomes soft and bouncy after 20 minutes points to heat-related damping fade, not a clicker baseline problem. Have the shock serviced and its nitrogen charge checked before another full moto.

Yes—the tire absorbs the first part of a bump, so pressure can make the suspension feel harsher or softer without touching a clicker.

- **Higher pressure:** firmer feel, more deflection over chop, but better rim and tube protection on sharp hits.
- **Lower pressure:** more compliance and grip, but too low feels vague or squirmy and risks rim strikes or pinch flats.

For your 2023 CRF450R, Honda’s baseline is **15 psi (100 kPa) front and rear, cold**. Establish that before judging the suspension. As general tuning practice, move about **1 psi at a time**: lower for smooth, slick ground or deep sand; higher for rocks, square edges and hard landings. Test the same section before changing clickers, and stop lowering at the first squirm or rim strike.

Pressure rises as tires heat up—don’t bleed a hot tire back down to the cold baseline. Tire pressure changes cushioning, not the fork or shock’s actual damping.

**Your shock spring is likely too soft**, assuming the suspension moves freely and both measurements are repeatable. You’ve needed enough preload to get 105 mm rider sag that the rear barely settles under the bike’s own weight.

GasGas specifies **105 mm rider sag and 35 mm static sag**; your 20 mm static sag is 15 mm short. Adding more preload won’t fix that balance—the usual fix is a stiffer shock spring, then resetting rider sag and checking static sag again.

First, repeat the static measurement after pushing the rear down and letting it rise, then lifting it and letting it settle. A substantial difference points to suspension friction that needs sorting before choosing a spring.

What shock spring rate is fitted, and what do you weigh in riding gear? Those determine how much stiffer to go.

On your 2023 CRF450R’s **standard shock spring 56 N/mm, anything shorter than 222.9 mm (8.78 in) installed length is too much preload**.

Measure the spring end-to-end between its seats with the rear wheel off the ground—not the exposed shock threads.

- Honda’s standard installed length: **232.3 mm (9.15 in)**.
- Allowed installed length: **222.9–233 mm (8.78–9.20 in)**.
- One adjuster turn changes spring length by **1.5 mm**: shorter adds preload and reduces sag; longer removes preload and increases sag. That is spring movement, not rear-wheel sag change.

Aim for **105 mm race sag** with full riding gear. If sag is still excessive at the minimum spring length, the spring is too soft; Honda’s optional stiff shock spring is **58 N/mm**. Very little bike-only sag after setting rider sag also points toward a spring that is too soft.

Preload changes ride height—it does not increase the spring’s rate.

Most ride-to-ride sag changes come from **measurement differences or suspension sticking**, followed by a preload collar moving or a new spring settling.

Your 2022 CRF250R’s standard rider sag is **105 mm (4.1 in) with the standard shock spring**.

1. **Make the measurement repeatable:** same riding gear, fuel level, level ground, helper and body position. Honda measures between the left rear fender bolt center and chain-adjuster locknut center: rear wheel hanging free, then rider aboard.
2. **Check for sticking:** with you aboard and supported by your helper, settle the rear once from being pushed down and once from being lifted. Different resting measurements point toward friction in the linkage, swingarm bearings or shock—not a preload adjustment.
3. **Check the collars:** put a witness mark across the preload adjuster and lock ring. Movement between rides identifies an adjuster that isn’t staying locked. Fresh suspension can also settle initially.

Hot shock oil changes damping feel, but shouldn’t substantially change settled static sag. Don’t chase it with clickers.

How many millimeters does it change between rides? If you find bearing play, knocking or a shock leak, fix that before riding.
Changing sag usually comes from inconsistent measuring, suspension friction, or a moving preload collar—not a spring changing rate between rides. Repeat the measurement under identical conditions before adjusting anything.

**Bleed them after practice and between motos**, with the front wheel off the ground—not with the bike’s weight on the forks.

1. Shut the engine off and support the bike securely on a stand so the forks extend fully. Let the forks cool before bleeding.

**Clickers adjust the tune you have; a revalve changes the tune’s underlying character.**

That lets a tuner target **easier movement over chop while retaining support under braking and on landings**, rather than simply making everything softer. There are still trade-offs.

The giveaway is when softening a clicker improves comfort but creates dive or bottoming—or adding support makes chop unbearable. A revalve addresses that compromise; it does **not** replace correct springs, sag or fixing binding parts.
Clickers fine-tune the existing damping; a revalve changes the damping curve itself, so the suspension can respond differently to small chop, braking loads and hard hits.

The main difference is **what holds the bike up—not whether there’s oil inside**.

- **Air fork:** A piston compresses trapped air as the fork moves down. That air pushes back harder as its volume shrinks, so resistance builds toward the bottom of the stroke. A negative-air chamber helps counter the initial force so the fork starts moving more easily.
- **Coil-spring fork:** Compressing a steel coil provides that supporting force. A straight-rate coil builds force more evenly through the stroke; trapped air above the oil still adds bottoming resistance.
- **Both:** Oil flows through pistons, shims and adjustable passages to control compression and rebound. Air pressure or coil rate supplies support; damping controls movement.

**Soft, intermediate and hard describe the dirt—not the rubber compound.** Choose for most of the lap, not one muddy corner.

| Terrain tire | Choose it when… | Why it works |
|---|---|---|
| **Soft** | Sand, deep loam or mud—you can easily push a finger into the dirt | Tall, widely spaced knobs dig in and clear mud |
| **Intermediate** | Packed loam, loose dirt over a firm base, or changing conditions | Balances digging grip with support on firmer sections |
| **Hard** | Dry, compacted or shiny ground that a finger won’t penetrate | Shorter, closely spaced knobs put more rubber against the surface |

A soft-terrain tire on hardpack can squirm and tear knobs; a hard-terrain tire in deep loose dirt struggles to dig in. Brand labels vary, so read the terrain description rather than judging by “soft” alone.

Set a known baseline before chasing upgrades or softer clickers. For your **2022 CRF250R**, assuming stock suspension:

1. **Rider sag: set to 105 mm (4.1 in)** in full riding gear, with fuel aboard. Measure from the rear wheel hanging free to rider aboard. Honda publishes no static-sag target; roughly 30–40 mm is general tuning guidance, checked with the bike resting under its own weight. Very little static sag at correct rider sag points to a shock spring that’s too soft.
2. **Fork: compression 12 clicks out; rebound 13 clicks out**, both legs equal—Honda’s standard reference.
3. **Shock: low-speed compression 6 clicks out, high-speed compression 2⅙ turns out, rebound 11 clicks out**—Honda’s standard reference. Count adjusters from gently seated, never forced.
4. **Tires: 100 kPa (15 psi) cold, front and rear.**
5. **Chain: 65–70 mm**, rear wheel off the ground, chain lifted; measure from the swingarm’s top to the chain-pin center at the rear end of the slider—not ordinary midpoint free play.
